title: Birchington Village Heritage Walk
surface: Pavements and tarmac paths with a short cliff-top section; Coleman Stairs has steps down to the beach (optional).
summary: A gentle loop from the station past Rossetti's grave, the Square, Crispe Park and the cliff-top streets where England's early bungalows were built.
description: This short circuit links the main stories of Birchington without leaving the village. From the station you walk down Station Road to the Square, the old heart of the village, where All Saints Church stands - the oldest building still standing in Birchington. The Pre-Raphaelite painter and poet Dante Gabriel Rossetti came here in 1882 hoping to recover his health and died soon afterwards; his grave, marked by a stone Celtic cross designed by Ford Madox Brown, is beside the south door, and a memorial window to him is inside. The route then heads north-east to Crispe Park, a small green that the council bought when Spurgeon's children's homes, which occupied Birchington Hall and its land from the 1920s until 1979, were sold for housing. Alpha Road and Epple Road bring you to Epple Bay. Turning west along the cliff top you reach Coleman Stairs and Spencer Road - the area where builder John Taylor and architect John Pollard Seddon put up some of the first bungalows in Britain in the 1870s and 1880s. Fair Outlook and the four Tower Bungalows are Grade II listed. Beresford Gap gives a view over the next bay before Beach Avenue and Rossetti Road lead back to the library, home of the Birchington Heritage Trust museum, and the station.

title: Minnis Bay to Reculver Towers along the Sea Wall
surface: Concrete and tarmac sea wall all the way (shared with cyclists).
summary: Flat, traffic-free sea-wall walk across the old Wantsum Channel marshes to the twin medieval towers at Reculver.
description: One of the best-known walks from Birchington, this linear route follows the Northern Sea Wall west from Minnis Bay to Reculver. It is part of the Viking Coastal Trail and the King Charles III England Coast Path, and the surface is a firm concrete or tarmac wall the whole way, so it suits buggies and wheelchairs. Inland lie the flat grazing marshes of the former Wantsum Channel, the sea strait that once made Thanet an island; seaward there is shingle, sand and wide views out to the offshore wind farm. The wall passes the outfalls of the Brooksend Stream and the River Wantsum before the twin towers of Reculver grow on the horizon. They are what remains of St Mary's Church, founded in 669 inside the Roman fort of Regulbium and pulled down in 1809; Trinity House bought the towers in 1810 and kept them as a landmark for shipping. Reculver also has a visitor centre, a pub and buses back towards Herne Bay and Birchington, or you can simply walk back the way you came (about 12 km in all). There is no shelter on the wall, so take water and something warm.

title: Birchington to Westgate-on-Sea by the Bays
surface: Concrete undercliff promenade, a cliff-top road section in Westgate and concrete promenade round St Mildred's Bay.
summary: Bay-hopping along the foot of the chalk cliffs from Minnis Bay past Grenham, Beresford Gap and Epple Bay to St Mildred's Bay.
description: This linear walk strings together the sandy bays between Birchington and Westgate. From Minnis Bay a concrete promenade runs east along the foot of the low chalk cliffs, past Grenham Bay and Beresford Gap, to the sheltered cove at Epple Bay. Here the lower walkway stops, so the route climbs to the cliff top and follows Sea Road into Westgate, with open views across the water. At West Bay you drop back to the promenade, which curves around the headland to St Mildred's Bay, a popular family beach with a cafe. The whole stretch is part of the Thanet Coastal Path and the Viking Coastal Trail. Westgate-on-Sea station is a short walk inland, so you can return to Birchington by train, or retrace your steps. Look out for rock pools on the chalk platforms at low water.

title: Westgate-on-Sea to Margate via Westbrook
surface: Promenade (concrete and tarmac) and seafront pavements.
summary: Seafront stroll from Westgate past the Sunken Gardens and Westbrook Bay to Margate Sands, Turner Contemporary and the Harbour Arm.
description: From Westgate station walk down to St Mildred's Bay and pick up the promenade heading east. It passes below the Royal Esplanade with the Sunken Gardens above, then runs along Westbrook Bay, a sandy beach in Margate's western suburb. Beyond Westbrook the promenade reaches the Nayland Rock shelter, a listed seafront shelter where T. S. Eliot wrote part of The Waste Land while recovering his health in Margate. Margate Main Sands opens up in front of the town, and the Jubilee Clock Tower, built for Queen Victoria's Golden Jubilee in 1887, marks the centre of the seafront. Continue past the Old Town to Turner Contemporary, the gallery built where the lodging house that Turner used once stood, and finish on the Harbour Arm, the stone pier with cafes and the visitor information centre at the Droit House. Margate station is a short walk back along the front.

title: Birchington to Quex Park Circular
surface: Pavement along Park Lane, estate drives and tracks, short public footpaths back into the village.
summary: Short loop from the village church to the Quex Park estate, home of the Powell-Cotton Museum and the Waterloo Tower.
description: Quex Park sits just south-east of Birchington: around 250 acres of parkland and gardens plus a large farmed estate. This loop leaves the church and follows Park Lane out of the village to the estate entrance, where Quex Barn farm shop and restaurant, the craft village and other attractions are grouped. Quex House, a Regency house that replaced an earlier mansion after 1814, holds the Powell-Cotton Museum, founded in 1896 by Major Percy Powell-Cotton to show the animals and objects he collected in Africa and Asia; it is famous for its natural history dioramas. Entry to the museum, house and gardens (lawns, a woodland walk and a walled kitchen garden) is by ticket, and in 2026 they open from mid-February to 1 November on selected days. The estate also contains the Waterloo Tower, a Grade II listed bell tower built by John Powell Powell with a later cast-iron spire. The walk returns along the estate drive to Park Road and short public footpaths back to Park Lane. Stay on the drives and paths and follow estate signs.

title: Minnis Bay and Brooks End Marshes Circular
surface: Sea wall, then grass and earth field paths, farm tracks and bridleways; can be muddy after rain.
summary: Sea wall and marsh loop over the drained Wantsum Channel, out along the coast and back by bridleways past the hamlet of Brooks End.
description: This loop gives a feel for the low, open country west of Birchington that was once under the sea. Brooks End, a hamlet now absorbed into Birchington about 1.6 km (1 mile) south-west of the centre, stands on land that was part of the Wantsum Channel, and is probably named after the many brooks that drain the area. The walk starts along the concrete Northern Sea Wall from Minnis Bay as far as the Brooksend Stream outfall, then turns inland on public footpath TE1 beside a drainage dyke across the grazing marsh. Bridleways TE12 and TE12A lead east along the edge of higher ground with wide views over the marsh, passing close to Little and Great Brooksend farms. Footpaths TE14 and TM35 then take you north-west across the fields back to the sea wall and Minnis Bay. Expect birds of farmland and marsh, big skies and very little shelter. Field paths can be wet and overgrown in places; check the Kent rights-of-way map if a path looks closed.

title: Reculver Country Park to Bishopstone Glen
surface: Grass-paver cycle path and grassy cliff-top paths; gentle climb west of the towers.
summary: Out-and-back along the cliffs of Reculver Country Park from the Roman fort and twin towers to the wooded Bishopstone Glen.
description: Reculver Country Park is a 64-acre coastal reserve run by Canterbury City Council and Kent Wildlife Trust, known for its protected soft cliffs, wildlife and fossils. Start at the visitor centre, which has displays on local history and wildlife, and walk out to the twin towers - the remains of St Mary's Church, founded in 669 inside the Roman fort of Regulbium, which guarded the Wantsum Channel. The church was demolished in 1809 and the towers were kept by Trinity House as a navigation mark. Then head west on the Oyster Bay Trail, which climbs gently along the cliff top with views back to the towers and out to sea; during the Second World War prototype bouncing bombs were tested off this coast. The path continues to Bishopstone Glen, a small wooded valley cutting through the cliffs, with a viewpoint. Return the same way, or carry on along the coast path towards Herne Bay.

title: St Nicholas-at-Wade, Wantsum and Reculver Loop
surface: Village lanes, farm tracks, grassy field paths and concrete sea wall; two railway crossings.
summary: Long, flat loop from the village across the Wantsum marshes to the Reculver towers and back along the Northern Sea Wall.
description: A big-sky walk across the former Wantsum Channel that links the old village of St Nicholas-at-Wade with Reculver. From the church walk out along Court Road and Potten Street Road to the hamlet of Chambers Wall, then follow farm tracks and field paths north-west over the marsh, crossing the railway (take great care at the foot crossings) and the River Wantsum. A path beside the railway leads to the Rushbourne sea wall, which brings you to the coast and the twin towers at Reculver - the remains of a 7th-century church within a Roman fort. The return follows the Northern Sea Wall east for about 4 km with the shingle shore on one side and grazing marsh on the other, before footpath TE1 heads back inland, over the railway again, to Shuart Lane and a footbridge over the A299 Thanet Way into the village. The route is based on a published loop that starts at Reculver; you can equally start there. Allow most of a day with a stop at Reculver.

title: Margate Old Town and Seafront Heritage Walk
surface: Pavements, cobbled Old Town streets, promenades and lower promenade; some steps.
summary: From the station along Margate Sands into the Old Town, the Shell Grotto, Turner Contemporary, the Shell Lady and the Walpole Bay tidal pool.
description: Margate grew into London's favourite seaside escape, and this loop takes in the highlights of that story. From the 1926 listed station walk down to the Nayland Rock shelter and along Margate Sands to the Jubilee Clock Tower of 1887. The Old Town begins behind the seafront: Duke Street and Market Place have cafes and independent shops, and the Margate Museum sits on the square. Climb through the streets to the mysterious Shell Grotto on Grotto Hill, an underground passage lined with millions of shells discovered in 1835 whose origin is still unknown, then return to King Street and the Tudor House, thought to have been a wealthy farmer's home. Turner Contemporary stands where the lodging house used by J. M. W. Turner once was, and the Harbour Arm (built 1812-15 by John Rennie) ends at the Shell Lady, a bronze honouring Turner's landlady Sophia Booth. The return heads east along the lower promenade beneath the cliffs past the old Lido to the Walpole Bay tidal pool, then back along the cliff-top Eastern Esplanade and Fort Crescent to Dreamland and the station.

title: Botany Bay to Broadstairs by the Chalk Cliffs
surface: Grass cliff-top paths, quiet roads around North Foreland, promenade at Stone Bay; steps at some bays.
summary: The 'Seven Bays' cliff walk: Botany Bay's chalk stacks, Kingsgate Bay and castle, Joss Bay, North Foreland lighthouse, Stone Bay and Viking Bay.
description: Thanet's most dramatic stretch of chalk coast. Botany Bay, at the end of Percy Avenue in Kingsgate, has white cliffs and chalk stacks left behind as arches collapsed. A cliff-top path leads past part of the North Foreland golf course and flint follies built by Lord Holland in the 18th century to Kingsgate Bay, reached only by steps, with the Captain Digby inn above it. Kingsgate Castle, built for Lord Holland and rebuilt in the 1860s, is now apartments. Joss Bay has lower cliffs and a fine stretch of sand; it is said to be named after a local smuggler or an old farm. Beyond it the cliffs rise to North Foreland, where a light has warned ships since at least 1499; the present lighthouse became the last in the UK to be automated, in 1998. Past the private Foreland estate the route drops to Stone Bay and its lower promenade, then passes Bleak House - Dickens's holiday home when it was Fort House - above Viking Bay and the harbour in Broadstairs. Return by the Thanet Loop bus or extend the walk.

dogs: Seasonal dog bans apply on several beaches; the cliff-top path is fine with dogs under control.
accessibility: Grass paths and some steps; cliff edges are unfenced and eroding.
tide_warning: If you choose to walk on the beaches between bays, check tide times: some sections are cut off at high water and the cliffs are prone to falls.

title: Broadstairs Dickens Town Walk
surface: Pavements and promenade with short steep paths and steps.
summary: A short loop around Viking Bay linking York Gate, the Dickens House Museum, Victoria Gardens, the Royal Albion and Bleak House.
description: Charles Dickens spent most summers in Broadstairs between 1837 and 1859, and this little circuit visits the places connected with him. Start at York Gate on Harbour Street, a defensive gateway of about 1540, and look at the harbour and its old jetty. A path climbs above Viking Bay to the Dickens House Museum on Victoria Parade, the cottage of Mary Pearson Strong, who inspired the character Betsey Trotwood in David Copperfield; it displays some of Dickens's possessions. Continue along the cliff top to Victoria Gardens and the bandstand, then Chandos Square with its flint-faced houses. Back along Victoria Parade you reach the Royal Albion Hotel, where Dickens stayed while working on Nicholas Nickleby, and the High Street. Albion Street and Fort Road lead up to Bleak House, known as Fort House when Dickens rented it and finished David Copperfield there (the house is viewed from outside). Finish down Harbour Street past the Old Curiosity Shop cafe. The Broadstairs Dickens Festival is held each June.

title: Ramsgate Royal Harbour and Pugin Walk
surface: Pavements, harbour-side roads and the tiled Kent Steps (steps can be avoided by the road).
summary: From the East Cliff down to the only 'Royal' harbour in Britain and up to the West Cliff, home of A. W. N. Pugin's house The Grange and St Augustine's church.
description: This walk follows the idea of the Pugin Town Trail from the East Cliff to the West Cliff. It begins on Victoria Parade, where a marble bust of Edward Pugin stands, then drops down Madeira Walk and the Kent Steps, whose colourful tiles added in 2020 are inspired by Augustus Pugin's designs. At the bottom is the Royal Harbour - the only British harbour allowed to call itself Royal, an honour granted after George IV's visit in 1820 - with the obelisk, the Royal Victoria Pavilion and the Maritime Museum. Pugin kept his lugger Caroline here. Walk along Military Road beneath the harbour arches and past the Sailors' Church, then climb Royal Parade to the West Cliff. Along St Augustine's Road you reach The Grange, the Grade I listed house Pugin designed for his family after buying the land in 1841 with a lookout tower over the sea, and next to it St Augustine's church, which he built and where he is buried in the chantry with his wife Jane.

title: Pegwell Bay to Ramsgate Coast Walk
surface: Country-park paths, cliff-top grass and tarmac paths, then West Cliff streets; two gates.
summary: England Coast Path stretch from Pegwell Bay nature reserve past the Viking ship Hugin and Pegwell village to Ramsgate's Royal Harbour.
description: A gentle section of the King Charles III England Coast Path. Pegwell Bay Country Park, beside the Sandwich and Pegwell Bay National Nature Reserve, has a cafe and toilets and looks over mudflats and saltmarsh rich in wading birds; at low tide a seal colony can often be seen near the mouth of the River Stour. The path follows the cliff top to the Hugin, a full-size replica longship that sailed from Denmark in 1949 to mark 1,500 years since the legendary landing of Hengist and Horsa. Continue past Pegwell village, where the Belle Vue Tavern is linked with smuggling stories and visits by Dickens, and along the Royal Esplanade on Ramsgate's West Cliff past St Augustine's church and The Grange, Pugin's home. Royal Parade then drops to the Royal Harbour, finishing at the obelisk by the Royal Victoria Pavilion. Please keep off the mudflats and saltmarsh, which are protected.

tide_warning: Do not walk out on the mudflats or the chalk at the cliff foot: the tide comes in quickly and the reserve has access restrictions.

title: Minnis Bay Accessible Sea Wall Stroll
surface: Smooth concrete and tarmac, flat throughout.
summary: Short, level out-and-back on the hard-surfaced sea wall from Minnis Bay, ideal for wheelchairs, buggies and short legs.
description: A simple, step-free stroll for anyone who wants sea air without hills or rough ground. From the promenade at Minnis Bay, a long sandy beach with a paddling pool and rock pools, head west onto the Northern Sea Wall. The surface is firm concrete or tarmac and the National Trail describes this stretch as suitable for buggies and wheelchairs. Within a few hundred metres the houses fall behind and the flat grazing marshes of the old Wantsum Channel open up inland, with Reculver's twin towers on the skyline ahead. Benches near the start make good resting points. Turn round at the Brooksend Stream outfall (about 1.1 km) or whenever you like, and return to the cafes at Minnis Bay. The wall is shared with cyclists, so keep to one side.

title: Turner and Dickens Walk: Margate to Broadstairs
surface: Town pavements and the long St Peter's Footpath (tarmac and earth, partly bridleway) across fields.
summary: Waymarked inland route linking Margate's Turner gallery with Dickens's Broadstairs via the village of St Peter's.
description: The Turner and Dickens Walk joins two towns tied to two great figures: J. M. W. Turner, who painted Margate's skies, and Charles Dickens, who holidayed in Broadstairs. Starting at Turner Contemporary, the route passes through the Old Town's Market Place and climbs past Hawley Square, then leaves Margate on the old St Peter's Footpath, a long-established path that crosses open farmland between the two towns. It reaches the village of St Peter's, with its High Street, before following St Peter's Road and The Broadway into Broadstairs. The High Street runs down to the seafront above Viking Bay, close to the Dickens House Museum and the Royal Albion Hotel. The walk is described as about 4 miles; buses link the two towns for the return.

title: Margate to Botany Bay via Cliftonville
surface: Concrete lower promenade below the cliffs, then cliff-top grass and paths beyond Foreness Point.
summary: Below the Cliftonville cliffs past the Walpole Bay tidal pool and Palm Bay to Foreness Point and the chalk stacks of Botany Bay.
description: This walk follows the first half of the Margate to Broadstairs coast route. From Turner Contemporary head east along the lower promenade beneath Fort Hill and the Cliftonville cliffs, past the old Lido to Walpole Bay, where a large tidal bathing pool is refilled by every tide. The promenade continues past Palm Bay, a quieter sandy bay, to Foreness Point, the headland at the entrance to the Thames Estuary. From here a cliff-top path leads on to Botany Bay, famous for its white chalk stacks and cliffs. Most of the route is on firm, flat paths. Continue to Kingsgate and Broadstairs on the Botany Bay to Broadstairs walk, or catch a bus back.
